author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
chunk_file: outputs/chunks/Made to Stick - Chip and Dan Heath/chunk_001.txt
title: Stories make ideas easier to remember and retell
what_it_says: Stories are easier to understand, remember, and retell than abstract explanations.
how_to_apply: Create a clear sequence of events.
Make the outcome easy to retell.
when_to_use: When explaining an idea people need to remember.
When trying to make information easier to retell.
When communicating with a broad audience.
when_not_to_use: When precision matters more than memorability.
When a technical specification is required.
tradeoffs: Stories improve recall but may simplify complex ideas.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
chunk_file: outputs/chunks/Made to Stick - Chip and Dan Heath/chunk_009.txt
title: Use intent instead of detailed plans
what_it_says: In complex and unpredictable situations, detailed plans quickly become obsolete. A clear statement of intent allows people to adapt while remaining aligned with the desired outcome.
why_it_matters: Teams can respond to changing conditions without waiting for new instructions.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Army leaders replaced rigid plans with concise statements describing the desired end state.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Soldiers could improvise when circumstances changed.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Communicate outcomes rather than prescribing every action.

decision_rules.rule: State the desired outcome rather than every step.
decision_rules.condition: When operating in uncertain environments.
decision_rules.action: Communicate intent and allow local adaptation.
decision_rules.rationale: Unexpected events will invalidate detailed plans.

warnings.consequence: People cannot adapt effectively.
warnings.prevention: Define intent and empower execution.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When teams face uncertainty.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Works in business, education, product development, and military operations.

when_not_to_use: Highly predictable repetitive tasks
tradeoffs: Less control over specific actions in exchange for greater adaptability.
evidence: You can lose the ability to execute the original plan, but you never lose the responsibility of executing the intent.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
chunk_file: outputs/chunks/Made to Stick - Chip and Dan Heath/chunk_009.txt
title: Simplicity comes from identifying the core
what_it_says: Making ideas stick requires identifying the single most important idea and removing competing messages.
why_it_matters: People remember and act on focused ideas more effectively.

examples_from_source.example_name: Commander's Intent as a single objective
examples_from_source.what_happened: Military leaders identify one overriding objective.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Everyone can align around the same goal.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Choose one primary message.

decision_rules.rule: Prioritize one core message.
decision_rules.condition: When communicating an idea.
decision_rules.action: Remove secondary messages that compete with the main point.
decision_rules.rationale: People cannot focus on several 'most important' ideas simultaneously.

patterns.description: Reduce information until only the essential idea remains.

warnings.warning: Too many priorities dilute the message.
warnings.consequence: People struggle to remember or act.
warnings.prevention: Choose one core objective.

when_not_to_use: When detailed technical reference material is required
tradeoffs: Some nuance is sacrificed for clarity.
evidence: You can't have five most important goals.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
chunk_file: outputs/chunks/Made to Stick - Chip and Dan Heath/chunk_010.txt
title: A simple core principle can coordinate complex organizations
what_it_says: Organizations can align thousands of decisions by establishing a simple core idea that employees use as a decision filter.
why_it_matters: People can act independently while remaining aligned with organizational goals, reducing the need for detailed rules and oversight.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Herb Kelleher instructed employees to evaluate decisions by asking whether they helped Southwest remain the low-fare airline.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The principle enabled employees to make decisions without needing executive approval.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Create a simple decision filter that employees can apply to everyday choices.

examples_from_source.what_happened: A proposed menu addition was evaluated against Southwest's low-fare mission.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The idea was rejected because it did not support the core objective.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Evaluate new initiatives based on whether they advance the primary objective.

decision_rules.rule: Test decisions against the core mission.
decision_rules.condition: When evaluating a new initiative or request.
decision_rules.action: Ask whether it directly supports the organization's primary objective.
decision_rules.rationale: Resources should reinforce the central strategic goal.

patterns.description: Use a simple organizational principle to guide decentralized decisions.
steps: Reject actions that conflict with it.

warnings.warning: Do not confuse simplicity with dumbing down.
warnings.consequence: Important strategic clarity may be replaced with oversimplification.
warnings.prevention: Focus on prioritization and elegance rather than reducing complexity for its own sake.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When coordinating teams or scaling decision-making.
steps: Translate it into a decision question.
Train people to use the question independently.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: The mission should be specific enough to eliminate ambiguity.

when_not_to_use: Situations requiring highly detailed procedural instructions
tradeoffs: Simple principles improve speed but may not capture every nuance.
evidence: "We are THE low-fare airline."

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
chunk_file: outputs/chunks/Made to Stick - Chip and Dan Heath/chunk_010.txt
title: Communicate the most important idea first
what_it_says: Effective communication starts with the most important information and organizes supporting details afterward.
why_it_matters: Audiences receive the key message even if they stop reading or listening before the end.

examples_from_source.what_happened: News stories begin with the most important information in the lead.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Readers quickly understand the core message.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Lead with the central idea before providing context.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Information is organized from most important to least important.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Readers retain critical information regardless of how much they consume.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Structure communication according to importance.

decision_rules.rule: Identify the core message before communicating.
decision_rules.condition: When writing, presenting, or explaining information.
decision_rules.action: Place the most important point first.
decision_rules.rationale: Audiences may not consume the entire message.

patterns.description: Organize information from highest importance to lowest importance.

warnings.consequence: Audiences may miss the most important message.
warnings.prevention: Determine the central idea before focusing on details.

application_patterns.when_to_use: Writing reports, presentations, articles, or executive summaries.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Particularly useful when audience attention is limited.

when_not_to_use: Narratives designed to create suspense
tradeoffs: Improves clarity but may reduce dramatic storytelling impact.
evidence: "The first sentence, called the lead, contains the most essential elements of the story."

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
chunk_file: outputs/chunks/Made to Stick - Chip and Dan Heath/chunk_010.txt
title: A clear commander's intent enables decentralized decision making
what_it_says: Organizations can coordinate thousands of independent decisions when everyone understands a simple core objective. A concise commander's intent acts as a decision filter that helps employees evaluate opportunities and tradeoffs without requiring constant management oversight.
why_it_matters: Teams operate in environments filled with unexpected situations. A clear intent allows people to make aligned decisions even when no explicit rule exists.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Herb Kelleher instructed employees that Southwest was 'THE low-fare airline.' When a proposal was made to serve chicken Caesar salads, the decision was evaluated against whether it strengthened the company's low-fare position.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: A single strategic principle provided a consistent way to judge operational decisions.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Create a simple strategic statement that employees can use to evaluate new ideas and requests.

decision_rules.rule: Evaluate actions against the core objective.
decision_rules.condition: When considering a new initiative, feature, or request.
decision_rules.action: Ask whether the proposal directly advances the organization's primary goal.
decision_rules.rationale: Resources should support the core strategy rather than create distractions.

patterns.description: Use a central strategic objective as a filter for decentralized decisions.
steps: Approve actions that reinforce the objective.
Reject actions that weaken or distract from it.

warnings.warning: Multiple competing priorities can weaken decision quality.
warnings.consequence: Employees may make inconsistent choices and lose strategic alignment.
warnings.prevention: Keep the primary objective clear and easy to apply.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When teams must make independent decisions in dynamic environments.
steps: Use it as a recurring decision filter.
Train employees to reference it during tradeoff discussions.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Works for companies, projects, products, teams, and leadership situations.

when_not_to_use: situations requiring detailed technical instructions
highly regulated tasks that require strict procedural compliance
tradeoffs: Simple strategic guidance increases flexibility but may omit operational details.
evidence: Kelleher's Commander's Intent is 'We are THE low-fare airline.'

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
chunk_file: outputs/chunks/Made to Stick - Chip and Dan Heath/chunk_010.txt
title: Simplicity is prioritization, not simplification
what_it_says: Effective simplicity comes from identifying and emphasizing the most important idea rather than reducing complexity through oversimplification or dumbing down.
why_it_matters: People often misunderstand simplicity as removing sophistication. The real challenge is deciding what matters most.

examples_from_source.what_happened: The company reduced its strategic focus to being 'THE low-fare airline.'
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The message remained powerful because it clarified priorities rather than removing complexity.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Distill communication to the most important priority before adding supporting details.

decision_rules.rule: Prioritize before simplifying.
decision_rules.condition: When crafting a message or strategy.
decision_rules.action: Identify the single most important idea first.
decision_rules.rationale: Clarity emerges from prioritization, not from merely using simpler words.

warnings.consequence: Important nuance may be removed without improving clarity.
warnings.prevention: Focus on identifying the core message rather than reducing intellectual depth.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When creating messaging, presentations, product narratives, or strategic plans.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful for writing, teaching, marketing, and leadership communication.

when_not_to_use: situations where all details carry equal importance
tradeoffs: Strong prioritization increases clarity but may leave secondary information unexplored.
evidence: They're simple because they reflect the Commander's Intent. It's about elegance and prioritization, not dumbing down.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
chunk_file: outputs/chunks/Made to Stick - Chip and Dan Heath/chunk_010.txt
title: Lead with the most important information
what_it_says: Journalists use the inverted pyramid structure by presenting the most important information first and placing supporting details afterward. This maximizes understanding regardless of how much attention the audience gives the content.
why_it_matters: People often stop reading before reaching the end. Presenting the core message first ensures it is received even when attention is limited.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Journalists place the most important information in the lead and organize subsequent details in decreasing order of importance.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Readers gain the most critical information even if they do not finish the article.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Place the core message at the beginning of communications.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Reporters transmitted the most important information first because communication lines could be interrupted at any moment.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The structure evolved as a practical solution to uncertainty and limited attention.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Assume communication may be interrupted and lead with what matters most.

decision_rules.rule: Communicate the most important information first.
decision_rules.condition: When writing articles, presentations, reports, or messages.
decision_rules.action: Start with the core message before supporting details.
decision_rules.rationale: Audiences may not consume the entire communication.

patterns.description: Structure communication from highest importance to lowest importance.

warnings.consequence: Audiences may miss the main point or lose interest before reaching it.
warnings.prevention: Identify the core message and place it at the beginning.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When readers, users, customers, or teams may only consume part of a message.
steps: Place optional details near the end.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in writing, presentations, product updates, marketing, and executive communication.

when_not_to_use: mystery narratives
stories where suspense is intentionally preserved
tradeoffs: Leading with the conclusion improves clarity but may reduce suspense and narrative tension.
evidence: The inverted pyramid structure—the most important info is at the top.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Finding the core requires forced prioritization
what_it_says: Communicators often lose sight of the core message because they become immersed in details and complexity. Finding the core requires choosing one central idea and resisting the temptation to communicate everything at once.
why_it_matters: People cannot easily remember or act on multiple competing priorities. Clear communication depends on identifying and emphasizing the single most important message.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Journalists often become immersed in details and lose track of the most important element of a story, leading to buried leads.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The example shows how expertise and information abundance can obscure what audiences actually need to know.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: When communicating, identify the one thing the audience must remember before adding supporting details.

decision_rules.rule: Choose one core message.
decision_rules.condition: When multiple important ideas compete for attention.
decision_rules.action: Identify the single most important message and communicate it first.
decision_rules.rationale: A message with one clear priority is easier to understand and remember.

patterns.description: Reduce complexity by selecting one dominant idea.

warnings.warning: Do not allow details to overshadow the core message.
warnings.consequence: The audience may miss the most important point.
warnings.prevention: Continually evaluate whether each detail supports the central idea.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When explaining complex topics, strategies, products, or initiatives.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Applicable to writing, presentations, marketing, leadership, and teaching.

when_not_to_use: When the objective is comprehensive reference documentation
tradeoffs: Simplicity may omit nuance, but improves clarity and memorability.
evidence: There's only one lead, and there's only one core. You must choose.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Finding the core is not enough; it must be communicated
what_it_says: Organizations often know their priorities but fail to communicate them effectively. A core idea only becomes valuable when it is understood and applied consistently by others.
why_it_matters: Execution depends on shared understanding. Strategic priorities must be translated into messages that influence everyday decisions.

examples_from_source.example_name: Hoover Adams and local news coverage
examples_from_source.what_happened: Adams identified local focus as the newspaper's core priority and repeatedly communicated it to staff through memorable language and examples.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The organization aligned around a shared principle rather than relying on constant supervision.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Leaders must communicate priorities in a form that others can remember and apply independently.

decision_rules.rule: Translate priorities into memorable guidance.
decision_rules.condition: When a strategy must be executed by many people.
decision_rules.action: Convert abstract priorities into simple, repeatable messages.
decision_rules.rationale: People cannot consistently execute priorities they do not clearly understand.

patterns.description: Convert a strategic priority into a memorable communication tool.

warnings.warning: Assuming people understand priorities because leadership understands them.
warnings.consequence: Teams make inconsistent decisions.
warnings.prevention: Communicate priorities repeatedly in memorable forms.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When leading teams or implementing strategy.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful for leadership, operations, product teams, and change initiatives.

when_not_to_use: Highly technical procedures requiring detailed instructions
tradeoffs: Simple messages improve alignment but may not capture every nuance.
evidence: Finding the core isn't synonymous with communicating the core.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Concrete phrases become decision-making tools
what_it_says: Simple and concrete phrases help people make consistent decisions because they translate abstract priorities into practical guidance.
why_it_matters: People can apply concrete instructions more easily than abstract principles.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Hoover Adams reduced the newspaper's strategy to a simple phrase that guided thousands of editorial decisions.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The phrase provided clarity across many situations without requiring detailed oversight.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Create memorable phrases that employees can use as decision filters.

decision_rules.rule: Express priorities in concrete language.
decision_rules.condition: When people must make independent decisions.
decision_rules.action: Use tangible words and examples rather than abstractions.
decision_rules.rationale: Concrete ideas are easier to understand and apply.

patterns.description: Turn a strategic objective into a memorable phrase.

warnings.consequence: Employees interpret priorities differently.
warnings.prevention: Use concrete, specific language.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When teams make frequent decentralized decisions.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Works in leadership, product development, customer service, and operations.

when_not_to_use: Situations requiring detailed technical specifications
tradeoffs: Concrete phrases improve execution but may oversimplify complex realities.
evidence: "Names, names, and names" is a simple statement that is symbolic of a core truth.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Simple messages are both core and compact
what_it_says: Effective simplicity requires both identifying the core idea and expressing it in a compact form.
why_it_matters: Compact messages are easier to remember, communicate, and apply.

examples_from_source.what_happened: A complex editorial philosophy was compressed into three repeated words.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The message remained memorable without losing its strategic meaning.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Reduce ideas to their smallest useful form while preserving meaning.

decision_rules.rule: Compress ideas without losing the core.
decision_rules.condition: When communicating important priorities.
decision_rules.action: Reduce unnecessary words while preserving meaning.
decision_rules.rationale: Lower information load improves memorability.

patterns.description: Combine prioritization with brevity.

warnings.consequence: Messages become short but meaningless.
warnings.prevention: Ensure compactness preserves the core message.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When creating slogans, principles, priorities, or positioning statements.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Applicable to branding, leadership, teaching, and marketing.

when_not_to_use: Legal or technical documents requiring precision and detail
tradeoffs: Compactness improves memorability but can sacrifice nuance.
evidence: Simple messages are core and compact.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Simple ideas require both a core and compact expression
what_it_says: A message becomes sticky when it combines a meaningful core idea with a concise form. Compactness alone is insufficient because short messages can be irrelevant, misleading, or empty.
why_it_matters: The goal is not brevity for its own sake but brevity that preserves and reinforces an important truth.

examples_from_source.what_happened: A complex editorial philosophy was compressed into a memorable phrase that still preserved its strategic meaning.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The phrase remained useful because it represented a genuine priority rather than a catchy slogan.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Compress ideas only after identifying the essential message.

decision_rules.rule: Compact ideas only after identifying the core.
decision_rules.condition: When creating memorable communication.
decision_rules.action: Reduce language while preserving the most important truth.
decision_rules.rationale: Compactness without substance creates empty slogans.

patterns.description: Create messages that are both meaningful and concise.

warnings.consequence: Messages become memorable but meaningless.
warnings.prevention: Ensure the message remains tied to a meaningful core.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When creating principles, slogans, positioning statements, or strategic guidance.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Applicable to leadership, branding, education, and product communication.

when_not_to_use: Situations requiring exhaustive explanation
tradeoffs: Compact messages improve recall but may sacrifice nuance.
evidence: Simple messages are core and compact.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Proverbs are compact decision-making tools
what_it_says: Proverbs survive because they encode practical wisdom into memorable rules of thumb that help people make decisions across many situations.
why_it_matters: People remember and apply simple guidance more easily than detailed instructions.

examples_from_source.example_name: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush
examples_from_source.what_happened: The proverb survived across cultures and centuries because it expresses a useful principle about preferring certainty over speculation.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Its longevity demonstrates the power of compact wisdom.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Distill experience into short principles that guide future decisions.

examples_from_source.what_happened: A simple statement became powerful enough to influence behavior across an entire lifetime.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Compact messages can guide action when they express important truths.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Simple guidance can shape behavior more effectively than lengthy explanations.

decision_rules.rule: Create principles that function like proverbs.
decision_rules.condition: When people need guidance across many situations.
decision_rules.action: Express wisdom as short, memorable rules.
decision_rules.rationale: People can recall and apply concise principles more easily.

patterns.description: Convert experience into a reusable rule of thumb.
steps: Distill it into a short statement

application_patterns.when_to_use: When establishing culture, values, or decision principles.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in leadership, operations, product development, and culture building.

when_not_to_use: Complex situations requiring detailed analysis

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Expertise creates resistance to simplicity
what_it_says: As expertise increases, people become more attracted to nuance and complexity and may view simplification as oversimplification.
why_it_matters: This tendency makes it harder for experts to communicate clearly with non-experts.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Experts fear that simplifying ideas will appear misleading or intellectually weak.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The fear discourages effective communication.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Communicators must separate necessary complexity from unnecessary complexity.

decision_rules.rule: Simplify without abandoning the core truth.
decision_rules.condition: When communicating expert knowledge.
decision_rules.action: Retain essential meaning while reducing unnecessary complexity.
decision_rules.rationale: Audiences need clarity more than exhaustive detail.

patterns.description: Increasing expertise leads to increasing communication complexity.

warnings.consequence: Messages become difficult for audiences to understand or apply.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When teaching, presenting, or explaining specialized topics.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Especially useful in education, consulting, product communication, and leadership.

when_not_to_use: Specialist-to-specialist technical discussions
tradeoffs: Simplification improves accessibility but may reduce precision.
evidence: That's when the Curse of Knowledge kicks in.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Simplicity requires actively resisting feature creep
what_it_says: Complexity accumulates naturally as people add features and capabilities. Preserving simplicity requires deliberate discipline and continuous prioritization.
why_it_matters: Without resistance, products and ideas become overloaded and lose effectiveness.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Jeff Hawkins limited the Palm Pilot to four core functions and rejected additional features that threatened simplicity.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The product succeeded by focusing on a few tasks and performing them well.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Define what something will not do as carefully as what it will do.

decision_rules.rule: Do a few things well.
decision_rules.condition: When designing products, services, or systems.
decision_rules.action: Reject additions that weaken the core purpose.
decision_rules.rationale: Additional features often reduce overall usability and focus.

patterns.description: Protect a core purpose from gradual complexity.

warnings.warning: Adding features because there is available capacity.
warnings.consequence: The product becomes harder to use and less effective.
warnings.prevention: Evaluate additions against the core objective.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When developing products, processes, services, or strategies.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Applicable to product management, operations, and communication.

when_not_to_use: Situations where functionality gaps genuinely prevent success
tradeoffs: Simplicity improves usability but may reduce feature breadth.
evidence: The Palm Pilot would do only four things, but it would do them well.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Visual reminders can reinforce strategic priorities
what_it_says: Physical objects can serve as memorable symbols of a core idea and help teams make consistent decisions.
why_it_matters: Visual reminders reinforce priorities more effectively than abstract instructions alone.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Jeff Hawkins carried a wooden block the size of the Palm Pilot and used it to challenge suggestions that added unnecessary features.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The block became a constant reminder of the product's commitment to simplicity.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Create visible symbols that reinforce important principles.

decision_rules.rule: Create visible reminders of priorities.
decision_rules.condition: When teams face repeated tradeoffs.
decision_rules.action: Use physical symbols to reinforce the core principle.
decision_rules.rationale: Concrete reminders help people remember and apply priorities.

patterns.description: Use a physical object to represent a core idea.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When leading teams, designing products, or driving change.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful for leadership, product teams, and organizational culture.

when_not_to_use: Situations where priorities are already universally understood
tradeoffs: Symbols improve recall but may oversimplify complex considerations.
evidence: The block of wood became a visual reminder to do a few things and do them well.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Meaningful concepts are easier to remember than raw data
what_it_says: People remember information more easily when it is connected to existing concepts rather than presented as isolated facts.
why_it_matters: Communication becomes more memorable when it links new information to familiar mental structures.

examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Meaning transforms disconnected data into memorable chunks.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Connect information to existing knowledge whenever possible.

decision_rules.rule: Package information into meaningful concepts.
decision_rules.condition: When teaching or communicating complex information.
decision_rules.action: Organize facts around familiar ideas or categories.
decision_rules.rationale: People remember concepts more easily than isolated details.

patterns.description: Group information into meaningful units.
steps: Connect it to a familiar concept

warnings.consequence: People remember less and learn more slowly.
warnings.prevention: Attach new information to existing mental models.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When teaching, training, writing, or presenting information.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in education, onboarding, documentation, and content creation.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Compact messages work by activating existing knowledge
what_it_says: People remember compact ideas because they function as pointers to knowledge that is already stored in memory rather than requiring entirely new information to be remembered.
why_it_matters: Communication becomes more efficient when it leverages what audiences already know.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Participants remembered JFK more easily than random letters because the concept already contained many stored associations.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Existing knowledge reduces memory load.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Anchor new communication to familiar concepts whenever possible.

decision_rules.rule: Use existing knowledge whenever possible.
decision_rules.condition: When communicating complex ideas.
decision_rules.action: Connect new information to concepts the audience already understands.
decision_rules.rationale: Existing mental structures reduce cognitive effort.

patterns.description: Use a small cue to activate a larger body of existing knowledge.

application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in education, marketing, onboarding, and communication.

tradeoffs: Leveraging existing knowledge improves comprehension but may create inaccurate assumptions if the analogy is weak.
evidence: You tap the existing memory terrain of your audience.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Schemas accelerate learning by connecting new ideas to known concepts
what_it_says: New concepts become easier to understand when they are explained through concepts that people already know.
why_it_matters: Schemas provide prebuilt mental structures that reduce the effort required to learn new information.

examples_from_source.what_happened: A pomelo was explained as a supersized grapefruit rather than through a detailed list of attributes.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The grapefruit schema enabled faster understanding and recall.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Introduce unfamiliar concepts through familiar reference points.

decision_rules.rule: Teach new ideas through existing schemas.
decision_rules.condition: When introducing unfamiliar concepts.
decision_rules.action: Link the new concept to a familiar category or example.
decision_rules.rationale: People learn faster when they can build on existing knowledge.

patterns.description: Connect unfamiliar concepts to familiar concepts.
steps: Find a familiar analogy or category

warnings.warning: Explaining new concepts only through isolated attributes.
warnings.consequence: Learning becomes slower and less memorable.
warnings.prevention: Anchor explanations to familiar schemas.

application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in education, consulting, training, and product adoption.

when_not_to_use: When no relevant schema exists
tradeoffs: Schemas improve learning speed but may oversimplify important distinctions.
evidence: We've made it easier for you to learn a new concept by tying it to a concept that you already know.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Complexity can be built from layers of simple ideas
what_it_says: Complex knowledge does not require starting with complexity. It can emerge from a sequence of simple concepts introduced in the right order.
why_it_matters: People learn and retain complicated subjects more effectively when knowledge is layered progressively.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Teachers begin with a simple trade scenario involving apples and oranges before introducing more advanced economic concepts.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Students develop foundational schemas that support future learning.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Teach difficult subjects by progressively building on simple foundations.

decision_rules.rule: Build complexity gradually.
decision_rules.condition: When teaching complicated subjects.
decision_rules.action: Introduce simple foundational concepts before advanced ones.
decision_rules.rationale: Foundational schemas support deeper understanding.

patterns.description: Develop complex understanding through staged learning.

warnings.consequence: Learners become overwhelmed and retain less information.
warnings.prevention: Create foundational schemas first.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When teaching, onboarding, or explaining sophisticated topics.
steps: Connect new layers to existing schemas
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in education, consulting, product training, and documentation.

when_not_to_use: When learners already possess advanced schemas
tradeoffs: Layering improves comprehension but may require more time than direct explanation.
evidence: It is possible to create complexity through the artful use of simplicity.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Schemas can be stretched to create complexity
what_it_says: Complex knowledge can be built by repeatedly adapting and extending simple schemas rather than introducing complexity all at once.
why_it_matters: People learn difficult subjects more effectively when new ideas are built on foundations they already understand.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Students first learn trade through a simple apples-and-oranges scenario, then adapt that schema to more advanced situations.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The schema provides a foundation for increasingly sophisticated understanding.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Build advanced knowledge by modifying simple foundational models.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Students begin with idealized pulley problems and later combine or stretch those schemas to solve more complex situations.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Complex reasoning emerges from reusable building blocks.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Introduce simple models first, then increase complexity gradually.

decision_rules.rule: Teach complexity through progressive schema expansion.
decision_rules.condition: When introducing difficult subjects.
decision_rules.action: Start with simple models and extend them incrementally.
decision_rules.rationale: People learn faster when complexity builds on existing understanding.

patterns.description: Create complex understanding by extending simple mental models.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When teaching, onboarding, or explaining technical concepts.
steps: Connect each addition to the existing model
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in education, training, consulting, and product onboarding.

when_not_to_use: When the audience already possesses advanced schemas
tradeoffs: Progressive learning improves comprehension but may require more time.
evidence: Schemas help us create complex messages from simple materials.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Accessibility is often more valuable than perfect accuracy
what_it_says: Communication should prioritize usefulness and comprehension over perfect technical accuracy when audiences cannot yet understand the more precise explanation.
why_it_matters: An idea that people can understand and apply is more valuable than a perfectly accurate explanation that they cannot use.

examples_from_source.example_name: Solar system model of the atom
examples_from_source.what_happened: Students are taught that electrons orbit the nucleus like planets orbit the sun even though this model is not fully accurate.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The simplified analogy helps learners build understanding before encountering more advanced explanations.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Use simplified models when they help people make sense of unfamiliar ideas.

examples_from_source.what_happened: The technically accurate explanation of electron probability clouds is less useful to beginners than the simplified planetary analogy.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Accessibility enables learning that would otherwise be impossible.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Provide only as much complexity as the audience can meaningfully use.

decision_rules.rule: Choose usefulness over exhaustive accuracy.
decision_rules.condition: When communicating with beginners or non-experts.
decision_rules.action: Provide the simplest explanation that enables understanding and action.
decision_rules.rationale: An unusable truth provides less value than a useful approximation.

patterns.description: Introduce a simplified model before revealing deeper complexity.

warnings.warning: Prioritizing accuracy to the point of uselessness.
warnings.consequence: Audiences fail to understand or apply the information.
warnings.prevention: Communicate only the complexity that is currently useful.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When teaching, onboarding, or presenting specialized knowledge.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in education, leadership, consulting, and technical communication.

when_not_to_use: When precision is legally, medically, or scientifically critical
tradeoffs: Accessibility improves understanding but may temporarily sacrifice precision.
evidence: Accuracy to the point of uselessness is a symptom of the Curse of Knowledge.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Analogies compress complex ideas into memorable pitches
what_it_says: Analogies allow communicators to express complex ideas quickly by linking them to concepts the audience already understands.
why_it_matters: A strong analogy can communicate meaning, structure, and expectations with very few words.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Movies were pitched using familiar references such as 'Die Hard on a bus' or 'Jaws on a spaceship.'
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The audience immediately understands the concept by combining existing schemas.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Use familiar reference points to explain unfamiliar ideas quickly.

decision_rules.rule: Use analogies to communicate complexity quickly.
decision_rules.condition: When explaining a new or abstract idea.
decision_rules.action: Combine the new idea with familiar concepts.
decision_rules.rationale: Existing schemas dramatically reduce explanation time.

patterns.description: Reduce a complex idea to a combination of familiar concepts.
steps: Combine them into a compact statement
Use the analogy as a communication shortcut

application_patterns.when_to_use: When presenting products, stories, strategies, or new concepts.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in marketing, product development, fundraising, and storytelling.

when_not_to_use: When the analogy introduces misleading assumptions
tradeoffs: Analogies improve comprehension but may omit nuance.
evidence: A great way to avoid useless accuracy, and to dodge the Curse of Knowledge, is to use analogies.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: High-concept pitches compress large amounts of meaning into familiar schemas
what_it_says: A strong pitch communicates a new idea by combining familiar concepts, allowing people to rapidly understand implications that would otherwise require extensive explanation.
why_it_matters: People can make decisions about unfamiliar ideas more quickly when those ideas are connected to existing mental models.

examples_from_source.example_name: Speed as Die Hard on a bus
examples_from_source.what_happened: A five-word description communicated the tone, budget, audience, style, and expectations of the movie.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The pitch transferred large amounts of understanding through a familiar reference.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Describe unfamiliar ideas through combinations of concepts people already understand.

examples_from_source.example_name: Alien as Jaws on a spaceship
examples_from_source.what_happened: The pitch immediately influenced design decisions about the setting, atmosphere, and characters.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The analogy guided creative decisions throughout development.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: A powerful analogy can align many decisions without detailed instructions.

decision_rules.rule: Explain new ideas through familiar concepts.
decision_rules.condition: When introducing unfamiliar products, stories, or strategies.
decision_rules.action: Combine the new concept with recognizable references.
decision_rules.rationale: Existing schemas accelerate understanding.

patterns.description: Communicate a new concept through a compact combination of familiar ideas.
steps: Combine them into a short phrase
Use the phrase to guide decisions

application_patterns.when_to_use: When pitching products, businesses, stories, or strategic initiatives.
steps: Test whether people understand the implications
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in marketing, fundraising, product strategy, and storytelling.

when_not_to_use: When no meaningful analogy exists
tradeoffs: Compression improves understanding but may omit nuance.
evidence: The compact, five-word phrase 'Die Hard on a bus' pours a breathtaking amount of meaning into the previously nonexistent concept of Speed.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Generative metaphors create new ways of thinking
what_it_says: Some metaphors do more than explain existing ideas. They become platforms that generate new insights, explanations, and innovations.
why_it_matters: Generative metaphors help people explore unfamiliar domains by borrowing structures from well-understood domains.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Psychologists used concepts such as memory, processors, and buffers from computing to develop theories about cognition.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The metaphor produced new questions and discoveries rather than merely explaining existing knowledge.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Use metaphors that generate new possibilities, not just explanations.

decision_rules.rule: Prefer metaphors that generate useful questions.
decision_rules.condition: When exploring complex or unfamiliar domains.
decision_rules.action: Choose analogies that reveal new possibilities and insights.
decision_rules.rationale: The best metaphors support both understanding and discovery.

patterns.description: Transfer structures from a familiar domain to generate insights in a new domain.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When solving problems, creating frameworks, or teaching abstract concepts.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in strategy, product design, education, and research.

when_not_to_use: When the metaphor creates misleading assumptions
tradeoffs: Generative metaphors stimulate insight but can oversimplify reality.
evidence: Good metaphors are generative.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: The best metaphors provide behavioral guidance
what_it_says: A useful metaphor helps people predict how they should behave in situations that were never explicitly described.
why_it_matters: Organizations scale more effectively when employees can derive behavior from shared principles rather than detailed instructions.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Disney consistently framed employees as cast members in a performance, shaping expectations about service, behavior, and customer interactions.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Employees could infer correct behavior without extensive rulebooks.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Choose metaphors that naturally imply desired behaviors.

examples_from_source.what_happened: The metaphor did not meaningfully guide employee behavior because artistry was not actually encouraged.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: A metaphor without behavioral implications becomes an empty label.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Avoid metaphors that sound appealing but do not influence decisions.

decision_rules.rule: Use metaphors that imply actionable behavior.
decision_rules.condition: When creating organizational values or cultural principles.
decision_rules.action: Select metaphors that naturally guide decisions and conduct.
decision_rules.rationale: Behavioral clarity creates consistency.

patterns.description: Create a metaphor that employees can use as a decision filter.

warnings.warning: Using symbolic labels that do not influence behavior.
warnings.consequence: The metaphor becomes decorative rather than useful.
warnings.prevention: Test whether people can derive decisions from the metaphor.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When building organizational culture or customer experience standards.
steps: Embed it in language and systems
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in leadership, customer service, culture design, and change management.

when_not_to_use: When the metaphor does not align with actual expectations
tradeoffs: Strong metaphors improve alignment but may constrain alternative interpretations.
evidence: This metaphor of employees as cast members in a theatrical production is communicated consistently throughout the organization.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Attention is captured by breaking expected patterns
what_it_says: People quickly adapt to familiar stimuli and stop noticing them. Unexpected changes force attention because the brain is highly sensitive to deviations from established patterns.
why_it_matters: Messages must disrupt expectations if they are to stand out in environments filled with repetitive communication.

examples_from_source.what_happened: A flight attendant replaced the standard safety announcement with humor and unexpected language, causing passengers to pay attention and applaud.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Breaking expectations transformed a routinely ignored message into an engaging one.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Interrupt familiar patterns when communicating important information.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Designers use blinking lights and changing siren patterns because constant signals are eventually ignored.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Variation keeps attention focused on important information.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Introduce change whenever sustained attention is required.

decision_rules.rule: Break a pattern to gain attention.
decision_rules.condition: When audiences are likely to ignore a familiar message.
decision_rules.action: Introduce an unexpected element that violates expectations.
decision_rules.rationale: Unexpected changes trigger attention automatically.

patterns.description: Capture attention by disrupting a familiar expectation.

warnings.consequence: Audiences stop noticing the message.
warnings.prevention: Introduce novelty or surprise.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When communicating in cluttered, repetitive, or low-interest environments.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in presentations, marketing, teaching, leadership, and safety communication.

when_not_to_use: When surprise would undermine trust or credibility
tradeoffs: Unexpectedness captures attention but can distract if unrelated to the message.
evidence: The most basic way to get someone's attention is this: Break a pattern.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Surprise gets attention while interest keeps it
what_it_says: Unexpectedness and interest serve different functions. Surprise captures attention initially, while interest sustains engagement over time.
why_it_matters: Effective communication requires both gaining attention and maintaining it long enough for the audience to absorb the message.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Humor and surprise initially attracted attention, while the entertaining delivery kept passengers engaged through the announcement.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Both surprise and interest were necessary for success.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Plan for both attention capture and attention maintenance.

decision_rules.rule: Use surprise to gain attention and interest to sustain it.
decision_rules.condition: When communicating ideas that require audience engagement.
decision_rules.action: Design messages with both an unexpected hook and a compelling continuation.
decision_rules.rationale: Attention alone is insufficient without continued engagement.

patterns.description: Move audiences from surprise into sustained interest.

warnings.consequence: Audiences notice the message but fail to stay engaged.
warnings.prevention: Build sustained interest after capturing attention.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When teaching, presenting, marketing, or storytelling.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful for presentations, writing, marketing, and education.

when_not_to_use: When audiences are already highly motivated and attentive
tradeoffs: Surprise improves attention but can become gimmicky if overused.
evidence: Surprise gets our attention. Interest keeps our attention.

author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
title: Unexpectedness can be deliberately designed
what_it_says: Unexpectedness is not purely accidental. Communicators can intentionally create surprise by violating audience expectations.
why_it_matters: Attention can be engineered rather than left to chance.

examples_from_source.what_happened: The authors note that even pausing unexpectedly or suddenly switching languages would have captured attention.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The mechanism is not entertainment itself but the disruption of expectations.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Design moments that violate audience assumptions.

decision_rules.rule: Create surprise by violating expectations.
decision_rules.condition: When attention is difficult to obtain.
decision_rules.action: Introduce a deliberate mismatch between expectation and reality.
decision_rules.rationale: The brain prioritizes unexpected information.

patterns.description: Create surprise through a controlled break from expectations.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When competing for attention in crowded environments.
steps: Connect the surprise to the message
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in advertising, teaching, presentations, and product launches.

when_not_to_use: When surprise creates confusion unrelated to the message
tradeoffs: Designed surprise improves attention but may distract if poorly connected to the message.
evidence: Our brain is designed to be keenly aware of changes.
